goodnight-jugnupur.skill: Sleep onset (settling from awake to asleep) through a calm, predictable wind-down
goodnight-jugnupur.headline: Young children fall asleep faster when the last part of the evening is calm, dim and the same every night — and a slow list of good-nights is exactly that.

findings.text: In a survey of mothers of 10,085 children across 14 countries (India included), a regular bedtime routine went with earlier bedtimes, falling asleep faster, fewer night wakings and longer sleep. The more nights a week the routine happened, the better the sleep.

Among the 3-to-5-year-olds in that survey, children with a routine every night fell asleep in about 18 minutes, against about 26 minutes for those who never had one, and slept about 10.2 hours a night against about 9.1 hours. This is a survey, so it shows a link, not proof that the routine caused the better sleep.

Young children are very sensitive to light before bed. In a lab study of 36 children aged 3 to 5, even dim room light (5 to 40 lux, about as bright as a few candles) cut melatonin (the body's 'time to sleep' hormone) by 78% on average. In more than half of the children, melatonin had still not come back 50 minutes after the light went off.
Screens are part of bedtime for many small children: a large review reports that 32% of toddlers watch television as part of their bedtime routine, and this has been linked to shorter, poorer sleep.

Children aged 3 to 5 need 10 to 13 hours of sleep in every 24 hours, naps included, according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's expert panel (with an American Academy of Pediatrics member on it).

In an Indian study of 368 children aged 1 to 3 in Chandigarh, 12.8% of parents said their child had a sleep problem, and 80.7% of children woke 1 to 3 times a night. The study was in toddlers, slightly younger than Chamku's listeners.

goodnight-jugnupur.how_story_uses_it: Chamku says good night to one thing at a time — mango tree, birds, pond, lotus, fish, ducks, fireflies dimming their lights — with the same short line each time, moving from the wide village down to the child's own room and body. The repeated pattern is predictable, the pace is slow, and the fireflies switching off one by one models the dimming lights that help melatonin rise.
goodnight-jugnupur.age_note: By age 4, most children can say what comes next in a story they know well, so a repeated 'Good night, ___' pattern is easy for them to join in and predict (CDC milestones). Children aged 3–5 need 10–13 hours of sleep in 24 hours, naps included.
goodnight-jugnupur.try_tonight: About an hour before sleep, dim the room lights and put screens away, then play this story as the very last thing. The CU Boulder team behind the light study suggests turning off screens and lowering home lights in the hour before bed.
goodnight-jugnupur.doctor: Children aged 3–5 need 10–13 hours of sleep a day, naps included; regularly getting less is linked to attention, behaviour and learning problems. If your child is often far below this, or snores most nights, raise it with your paediatrician — the AAP asks doctors to check for snoring at routine visits.

chamku-chaar-saansen.skill: Emotion regulation and calming the body (slow breathing to settle for sleep)
chamku-chaar-saansen.headline: A few slow breaths can calm a child's heart rate within a minute — the study that showed this used exactly four breaths.

findings.text: In a preregistered experiment with 342 children aged 5 to 12, a 1-minute cartoon video that guided children through four slow, deep breaths lowered their heart rate and raised a marker of the body's 'calm-down' system. A matching video without the breathing did not. These children were older than Chamku's listeners, so the effect in 3-to-5-year-olds is not yet tested.

A review of 15 studies in healthy adults found that slow breathing (fewer than 10 breaths a minute) is linked to a calmer body — steadier heart-rhythm changes (heart rate variability) — and to people feeling more relaxed and less anxious. These studies were in adults only.

Breathing is not magic for every moment. In a daily-life trial with 171 children aged 9 to 13, a slow belly-breathing exercise did not lift mood on average, but it did help children feel more relaxed at times when they were more worried than usual.

For preschoolers, the evidence on calming practices is mixed. A review of 18 studies of mindfulness programmes (which often include breathing games) in early childhood found mixed effects on self-control overall, with larger benefits for children who found self-control harder to begin with.

In a randomised trial with 68 preschool children, a 12-week mindfulness-based 'Kindness Curriculum' led to small-to-medium gains in flexible thinking and in waiting for a reward. The programme had many parts, so we cannot say how much came from breathing alone.

chamku-chaar-saansen.how_story_uses_it: Anaya says her body is full of 'popcorn' — a child's way of naming a busy, wide-awake body. Chamku turns four slow breaths into games (smell the flower, gently blow the candle, balloon tummy, bee hum, feather breath), and when Anaya blows too hard and sends Chamku flying, they laugh and try again more slowly. Each breath puts one 'popcorn' to sleep, so the child can count down to calm.
chamku-chaar-saansen.age_note: By age 3, most children can calm down within about 10 minutes after a parent leaves them, for example at a daycare drop-off (CDC milestones). Learning to calm down on purpose keeps developing through the preschool years, and young children still rely a lot on an adult to help.
chamku-chaar-saansen.try_tonight: Once your child is lying down, do four slow 'smell the flower, blow the candle' breaths yourself, slowly and out loud, and invite your child to copy — no pressure. The four-breath video study found calming effects even when children did not join in fully.
chamku-chaar-saansen.doctor: If your child snores often, breathes with effort, or gasps, snorts or pauses in breathing during sleep, tell your doctor: the American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children who snore often be checked for sleep apnea (blocked breathing during sleep).

paanch-kaam-bedtime.skill: Bedtime routine and self-care habits (following a fixed sequence of steps)
paanch-kaam-bedtime.headline: A short, same-every-night bedtime routine is one of the best-studied ways to help young children sleep — the benefits grow the more nights you do it.

findings.text: In a randomised trial of 405 families with children aged 7 months to 3 years, a simple 3-step bedtime routine improved how fast children fell asleep and cut night wakings, within three weeks.

In a survey of mothers of 10,085 young children in 14 countries, the benefits rose step by step with how many nights a week the routine happened, and the authors say 'the younger started the better'. Among 3-to-5-year-olds, only 44.9% had a routine every night.

Routines differ a lot between countries. In a sample of 29,287 children aged 0 to 3 from 17 countries or regions, having a routine on 5 or more nights a week ranged from 40% in India to 80% in the United Kingdom.

Experts group good bedtime routines into four kinds of activity: food, hygiene (bath, brushing teeth), talk (a story or song), and closeness (a cuddle). They suggest 2 to 4 calm activities lasting no more than 30–40 minutes. The American Academy of Pediatrics' 'Brush, Book, Bed' campaign links teeth, stories and sleep in one routine.
Brushing is worth building early: in a long-term study of 671 children, brushing rarely at age 3 predicted more tooth decay at age 15.

Routines may help more than sleep: children with regular routines at age 3 showed better control of feelings and behaviour, and talk-based routines like stories at age 3 were linked to stronger vocabulary at age 5. These are links found in observational studies, not proof of cause.

paanch-kaam-bedtime.how_story_uses_it: Anaya wants to jump straight into bed, and Brushu the toothbrush turns five bedtime jobs — toys, potty, wash, brush, pyjamas — into a counting game on her five fingers, with a cheerful 'Done! टिंग!' after each one. Funny moments (the teddy too round for the box, the toilet's 'burp') keep it light, and saying the same five steps in the same order each night is what makes it a routine rather than a list of orders.
paanch-kaam-bedtime.age_note: By age 5, most children can do simple jobs at home, such as matching socks or clearing the table, and by age 3 many can put on some clothes themselves, like loose pants (CDC milestones). So at 3–5, children can do parts of the routine on their own with an adult nearby.
paanch-kaam-bedtime.try_tonight: Pick 3 to 5 calm steps (for example toys away, potty, wash, brush, pyjamas, then a story) and do them in the same order tonight and every night, finishing within about 30–40 minutes. Keep the TV off during the routine.

chamku-light-off.skill: Problem solving and persistence (trying different ideas), with shared humour
chamku-light-off.headline: Children learn to keep trying when they see someone try hard, and laughing together seems to make learning stick.

findings.text: In a Science study of 262 babies aged 15 months, babies who watched an adult try several ways and work hard before succeeding then tried harder on a new, difficult toy than babies who saw the adult succeed easily. Watching effort changes how long children keep going.
Preschoolers test ideas like little scientists. When shown a confusing toy (average age 4¾), children explored it more, and 75% spontaneously tested each part on its own to work out what made it go.

Laughing may help learning. In a lab study with 18-month-olds shown a funny way to use a toy rake, 93.7% of the 16 babies who laughed then used the rake to get a toy, compared with 19% of the 21 who didn't laugh. The babies chose whether to laugh, so this shows a link, not proof that laughter caused the learning.
Laughter is social. In a small study of 20 children aged about 2½ to 4, children laughed eight times as much when watching a cartoon with another child as when watching alone.
Asking questions helps children solve problems. In a study of 67 four-year-olds working on a puzzle-like task, those who were allowed to ask questions did clearly better than those who could not.

chamku-light-off.how_story_uses_it: Chamku's light won't switch on, and he and Anaya try one idea after another — jumping, spinning, a phone charger, a big sneeze. Each try 'fails' in a funny way, but the sneeze gives a tiny spark, which is a clue that the light is inside and just 'asleep'. The story shows effort, testing ideas, using clues, and laughing together while you keep going.
chamku-light-off.age_note: By age 4, most children pretend to be something else during play, like a superhero or a dog (CDC milestones). A small study that followed four children found they already enjoyed jokes about 'impossible' things by 18 months, and a wide range of humour by age 3.
chamku-light-off.try_tonight: When something small goes wrong tomorrow (a lid that won't open, a toy that won't stand), think out loud: 'Hmm, that didn't work — let me try another way!' and try two or three ways before it works. Children who see an adult keep trying tend to keep trying themselves.

chand-race.skill: Wonder and early science thinking (the moon is very far away, so it seems to follow us)
chand-race.headline: 'The moon follows me' is one of the oldest findings in child psychology — and a gentle, real explanation is exactly what curious preschoolers are looking for.

findings.text: Nearly a hundred years ago, Jean Piaget found that if you ask children of 6 to 8 'What is the sun doing while you are walking?', they readily say that the sun and moon follow them. He saw this as part of young children's belief that nature acts on purpose.

Newer research is kinder to children's thinking. Children can tell natural things from human-made things, but they do like 'purpose' answers: 4- and 5-year-olds think it makes sense to say clouds are 'for raining'. This leaning tends to fade around ages 9–10.

When 60 school children were asked where the sun goes at night, many of the youngest (6–7 years) used simple, consistent 'models': 30% said the sun goes behind mountains or hills and 30% said it goes down into the ground. Children build their own theories of the sky and use them steadily.

The real reason: the moon is about 384,400 km (238,855 miles) away — roughly 30 Earths lined up. Houses and trees slide past the car window, but the moon is so far away that it stays in the same place in the sky, so it looks like it is keeping up with you.

Preschoolers want real reasons. In recorded conversations and an experiment with 42 children aged 3 to 5, children agreed and asked follow-up questions after a real explanation, but asked their question again when an adult gave a non-answer.

Playful testing is how preschoolers sort out confusing things: in one experiment (average age 4¾), 75% of children spontaneously tested each part of a puzzling toy on its own to find out what caused what.

chand-race.how_story_uses_it: Chamku races Chanda Mama to the mango tree, flies as fast as he can over the pond and fields, and every time he looks back the moon is still right above him. He even finds a second moon in the pond, and the Moon gently explains it is 'just my picture in the water'. The story keeps the wonder of the moon 'following' while planting the true idea: the moon is very, very far away.
chand-race.age_note: By age 3, most children ask 'who', 'what', 'where' or 'why' questions, and by age 5 most use time words like 'night' and 'tomorrow' (CDC milestones). Believing the moon follows you is normal well into the early school years.
chand-race.try_tonight: On the next clear night, stand with your child where you can see the moon and a nearby tree or lamp post. Walk ten steps together: the tree moves behind you but the moon stays put. Then give the real reason in one line — 'the moon is so far away it looks like it comes with us' — because preschoolers keep asking until they get a real explanation.

chamku-glow.skill: Early science understanding: real firefly biology (how the light works and blinking to talk), plus asking 'why'
chamku-glow.headline: Fireflies really do make their own light with body chemistry, switch it with a gas and oxygen, and 'talk' in flashes — so Chamku's facts are true science.

findings.text: Fireflies make their own light with a special helper molecule called luciferase (an enzyme: a tiny body-machine that speeds up a chemical reaction). It was the first light-making enzyme scientists ever copied, and doctors and scientists now use it in medical research.

Fireflies switch their light on and off with a gas called nitric oxide, working together with oxygen inside the light organ (the 'lantern'). That is why Chamku's 'air goes to a little room and — ting!' is close to the truth.
Fireflies really do talk in blinks. Scientists have found that female fireflies choose which male to answer by looking at his flash pattern.
Baby fireflies (larvae) live for months or even years, hunting snails and earthworms. Grown-up fireflies live only a short time and usually do not eat at all.
Bright lights at night are a known threat to fireflies all over the world. Of 150 kinds of firefly checked so far, about 20% face a higher risk of dying out.

Children's 'why, why, why?' is a learning tool. In recorded conversations and an experiment with 42 children aged 3 to 5, children were satisfied and asked follow-ups after real explanations, but repeated their question after non-answers.

chamku-glow.how_story_uses_it: Anaya guesses battery, switch and bulb one by one, and Chamku says no to each, then explains that when he breathes, air goes to a little room behind his tummy and his light comes on — 'bioluminescence', or in firefly language, 'ting!'. His hiccups make his light flicker, which is a playful hint that fireflies control their flashes, and the story ends with the blink game as firefly 'hello'.
chamku-glow.age_note: By age 3, most children ask 'who', 'what', 'where' or 'why' questions (CDC milestones), and many preschoolers keep asking until they get a real cause, not just 'because'.
chamku-glow.try_tonight: When your child asks 'why?', give a short, true reason ('Fireflies mix a special juice with air to make light') rather than 'just because', then ask 'What do you think?'. Preschoolers stay engaged and ask follow-ups when they get real explanations.

golu-gussa.skill: Emotion regulation (noticing anger and calming it down)
golu-gussa.headline: Anger is a normal part of being 3 to 5, and children calm down faster when a grown-up helps them name the feeling and practise a simple calm-down plan.

findings.text: Tantrums are normal at this age. In a study of 1,490 children aged 3 to 5, 83.7% had a tantrum in the past month, but only 8.6% had tantrums every day. Short outbursts after an expected upset, like a tower falling, were the ordinary kind.

A study of 211 children aged 1 to 6 in Thailand found the same picture: 95.3% showed at least one tantrum behaviour. Only 10.4% had tantrums lasting longer than 15 minutes, and 15.4% had them more than three times a week.

Naming the feeling helps. In 334 Chinese preschoolers (average age about 5), children who were better at naming feelings were rated by parents and teachers as better at calming down. In a 14-day diary of 181 of them, on days children put their feeling into words, they recovered faster that same day. This study shows a link, not proof of cause.

Parents can learn to coach anger. In a trial with 216 parents of 4- and 5-year-olds, a 6-session programme on emotion coaching (noticing, naming and talking through feelings) led parents to use more feeling words. Their children understood emotions better and had fewer behaviour problems, by parent and teacher report.

Calm-body practice in preschool shows promise, but the evidence is still early. In a randomised trial with 68 preschoolers, a 12-week mindfulness-based kindness programme improved social skills and school ratings. A larger trial of 245 children aged 3 to 5 found some but not all of the same benefits. We did not find a strong trial that tested deep breathing on its own at this age.

golu-gussa.how_story_uses_it: Golu's tower falls, which is exactly the kind of expected frustration that sets off ordinary tantrums. Chamku first says that everyone gets angry, then turns the feeling into three steps: say "I am angry" out loud (naming it), three slow counted stomps, and one long blow. When the wind comes back, Golu uses the steps by herself, which is how a practised plan becomes the child's own.
golu-gussa.age_note: Tantrums are most common between ages 1 and 3 and usually get better after 3 (AAP). Even so, most 3- to 5-year-olds still have one sometimes (83.7% in the past month in Wakschlag's study).
golu-gussa.try_tonight: Practise Golu's three steps as a game while your child is calm: say "I am angry!" in a big rhino voice, do three slow stomps, then one long blow. Next time real anger comes, name it for them first ("You're angry because the tower fell") and then do the steps together.
golu-gussa.doctor: Talk to your paediatrician if tantrums happen every day, often last longer than 15 minutes, come out of the blue, or involve hurting people or breaking things. In research, these patterns were much less common and marked the tantrums worth checking. The AAP advises talking with your paediatrician whenever you are worried.

chamku-rang-roshni.skill: Emotion vocabulary and labelling (naming happy, angry and sad)
chamku-rang-roshni.headline: Putting a feeling into words tends to make it lighter, and children who know more feeling words tend to get on better with other children.

findings.text: In a brain-scan study of 30 adults, naming the feeling in a picture (for example "angry") calmed the brain's alarm area, the amygdala, more than other ways of looking at the picture. This was shown in adults, not children.

The same idea has now been seen in young children. In 334 preschoolers in China (average age about 5), those better at naming feelings calmed down better. In a 14-day diary, on days children named their feelings, they recovered faster the same day. It is a link, not proof of cause.

Big upsets often mix two feelings. In reports on 335 tantrums of children aged 18 months to 5 years, anger and distress (whining, crying, wanting comfort) showed up as two separate parts. That is why a child can be angry and sad at the same time, as Anaya is.

Feeling words matter for friendships. A meta-analysis (a study that combines many studies) by Trentacosta and Fine found that across 42 studies, children who understood emotions better had better social skills; the average link was modest (r = .21).

How parents talk matters. Across studies of 2,298 children under 7, parents who talked more about thoughts and feelings had children with better understanding of emotions and minds. The links were small (r = .11 to .15), and talk that explained why someone felt something worked better.

Stories can grow feeling words. In a trial with 208 children about 8 years old, a story-reading programme about feelings increased emotion vocabulary and emotion knowledge. This was in older children, so for 3- to 5-year-olds it is a reasonable hope rather than proof.

chamku-rang-roshni.how_story_uses_it: Anaya will not talk at first, and Chamku does not push. He gives her one easy job: say the feeling's name. She says "angry" and then "sad", gives the reason (her tower fell and nobody saw), and says her heart feels lighter. Chamku's light turns each named feeling into a colour, which gives a young child a picture for a word.
chamku-rang-roshni.age_note: By age 4, most children comfort others who are hurt or sad and can talk about at least one thing that happened in their day. These are the building blocks for naming their own feelings.
chamku-rang-roshni.try_tonight: Play Chamku's light game: you say a colour, your child makes the matching face. Then each of you shares one feeling from today and why ("I felt sad when…"). Explaining the reason is the kind of talk linked to better emotion understanding.

aakhri-laddoo.headline: Fair sharing grows slowly between ages 3 and 8, and young children share more equally after they have worked together.

findings.text: Wanting it all is normal at 3 or 4. In a classic experiment with children aged 3 to 8, most 3- and 4-year-olds chose the selfish option, while most 7- and 8-year-olds preferred equal splits.

Teamwork brings sharing forward. In a lab experiment, 3-year-olds who had worked together with a peer to win rewards then shared them mostly equally, even when one child could easily have kept them all.

Children notice "I got less" long before "you got less". Children aged 4 to 7 turned down deals where they got less than a partner but accepted deals where they got more. Only 8-year-olds turned down both kinds of unfair deal.

This pattern shows up around the world. In 866 pairs of children aged 4 to 15 from seven countries, including India, objecting to getting less appeared in every country by middle childhood. Objecting to getting more came later and only in three of the seven.

Stories can nudge sharing, but details matter. Children aged 4 to 6 shared more stickers after a sharing story with human characters. The same story with animal characters did not increase sharing, though children who saw the animals as more human-like shared more.

aakhri-laddoo.how_story_uses_it: Anaya and Chiku fight over the last laddoo, which is normal at this age. Then they save the falling laddoo together, and only after that teamwork does Chamku suggest half-half. Anaya, a human child, gives the bigger half to Chiku because Chiku's tail helped. In experiments, children usually start refusing to take more than a friend only at about 8 or later, and not in every country. So the story shows this next step gently, without expecting it yet.
aakhri-laddoo.age_note: Most 3- to 4-year-olds still choose the bigger share for themselves. Most children prefer equal splits by about 7 to 8, though 3-year-olds can share equally after working together.
aakhri-laddoo.try_tonight: Do one small job together first, like setting out plates, and then share a snack half-and-half and say "मज़ा double!". Young children share more equally after they have worked together for something.

golu-ballet.skill: Confidence and self-concept (trying something your own way)
golu-ballet.headline: Praising what a child did, rather than what a child is, helps them keep trying after a wobble, though the long-term evidence is mixed.

findings.text: Small words make a difference. In an experiment with 24 children aged 4 to 5, hearing "You are a good drawer" led to more giving up and harsher self-judgment after mistakes than hearing "You did a good job drawing". It was a small study.

In 53 families filmed at home, the more parents praised effort when children were 14 to 38 months old, the more those children believed at 7 to 8 years that abilities can grow and liked challenges. This shows a link, not proof of cause.

Keep expectations realistic. Two large meta-analyses (273 studies with 365,915 people, and 43 studies with 57,155 people) found that belief in "I can grow" has only weak links with school results overall. Most of these studies were in older students. Process praise is a sensible habit, not a magic fix.
Children learn to keep trying by watching. In experiments with 262 babies aged 13 to 18 months, babies who saw an adult try again and again before succeeding then tried harder on a new, hard toy.
Showing off is a normal skill. By age 5, most children sing, dance or act for their family.

golu-ballet.how_story_uses_it: Golu thinks she is too big for ballet. Chamku does not say "you're a great dancer". He invites her to try her own way, and she keeps trying: toes, then a sit-down ballet, then a sneeze ballet. Before the show she says she is nervous, and Chamku stays close. At the end Golu names what she did: "I stayed Golu. My stomp, my jump, my sneeze, all my own."
golu-ballet.age_note: By 4, most children pretend and play roles, and by 5 most sing, dance or act for you.
golu-ballet.try_tonight: Put on music and do a Golu dance together. Afterwards, praise what your child did ("You made up such a big spin!" or "You kept going when you wobbled"), not a label ("You're a great dancer").

anaya-haar.skill: Frustration tolerance and handling losing (good sportsmanship)
anaya-haar.headline: Losing is hard for young children, and they learn to cope by watching grown-ups lose calmly and try again.

findings.text: Handling disappointment goes with getting along. In 78 preschoolers (average age 4.9), children with better self-control showed fewer signs of upset when given a disappointing gift. Parents, teachers and other children also saw them as better at making friends. This is a link, not proof of cause.

Big feelings at losing are common. In a small study of 14 kindergarten children, some became aggressive in the moment of losing a game. Over time, the whole group found their own ways to cope with losing.

Children copy how adults handle setbacks. In experiments with 262 babies aged 13 to 18 months, those who saw an adult try again and again then tried harder themselves on a new task. This was in babies, but it supports letting children see you lose and carry on.
Upsets in expected situations, like losing a game, are the ordinary kind. In a study of 1,490 children aged 3 to 5, these milder reactions were much more common than worrying ones.
Board games have a bonus. Preschoolers from low-income families who played a simple numbered board game for four 15-minute sessions caught up with better-off peers in their sense of numbers.

anaya-haar.how_story_uses_it: Anaya loses and nearly throws the dice. Chamku does not scold her. He tells her he loses too (to a snail!), shows his light dimming and a long breath, and says it is okay to feel sad for a little while. Then comes a simple ritual: "Good game" and a high five, and another round. The second time, the snakes are funny rather than unfair.
anaya-haar.age_note: By age 5, most children can follow rules or take turns when playing games with other children. At 3 and 4, turn-taking and losing are still being learned.
anaya-haar.try_tonight: Play one short board game. When you lose, say it out loud: "Oh, I lost. I feel a bit sad. Long breath… Good game!" Then high-five and offer another round. Children learn to handle setbacks from watching adults.

anaya-didi.skill: Adjusting to a new sibling (and early helping)
anaya-didi.headline: Most children adjust to a new baby without a crisis, and older children who get a real way to help tend to build a warmer bond.

findings.text: A new baby is usually not a crisis. A review of 30 studies found no strong evidence that the birth of a sibling is a crisis for most children. The clearest change was less affection towards the mother for a while. Children differed a lot.

Big brothers and sisters can help. Researchers watched 216 firstborns aged 13 to 70 months during a nappy change of their 1-month-old sibling to see how they cooperated. Children who were hard to soothe cooperated less, but mainly in families where parents undercut each other.

Early interest pays off. An earlier classic study (Dunn and Kendrick, 1982, as reported by Song and Volling) found that children who showed interest in the newborn and often helped at one month had a friendlier relationship with the sibling at 14 months.
Helping comes naturally. In a classic experiment, 22 of 24 toddlers aged 18 months helped an adult at least once, usually within seconds, and often before being asked.

Thank them; don't pay them. After being given a toy as a reward for helping, 20-month-olds later helped in 53% of chances, compared with 89% for children given no reward and 81% for children given praise.

Some going backwards is normal. The AAP says to expect an older child to regress a little (for example, toilet accidents or wanting a bottle), to invite them to help, and to keep special one-on-one time.

anaya-didi.how_story_uses_it: Anaya says what many older children feel: everyone looks at the baby and nobody plays with her. Chamku lets her feel it, then helps her find a job only she can do. She makes the baby laugh with peek-a-boo, puts on his sock and sings to him. When he holds her finger, being a didi becomes a special role instead of a loss.
anaya-didi.age_note: By age 4, most children like to be a helper and comfort others who are hurt or sad, so a small baby job fits this age well.
anaya-didi.try_tonight: Give your older child one small real baby job each day, like fetching a sock or singing to the baby, and thank them with words and a hug rather than a sweet. Add ten minutes of one-on-one time with just them.

anaya-school-bag.skill: Starting school: separation and making a first friend
anaya-school-bag.headline: A predictable goodbye and one friendly contact help children settle, and having friends in class is linked with liking school.

findings.text: Friends make school feel better. In a study of children starting kindergarten, those with more friends in class at the start of school liked school more. Children who made new friends did better in learning over the year.
A research summary for teachers noted that friendships predict good adjustment in the first weeks of kindergarten, and that making new friends shifts a child's adjustment in a positive direction.

Settling in takes a few days, and it goes better when it is gradual. In 70 toddlers aged 15 months starting childcare, stress hormone levels in the first hour after the mother left were 75% to 100% higher than at home during the first days. Bonds stayed secure when mothers spent more days settling them in. This was in toddlers, not 3- to 5-year-olds.

Short, predictable goodbyes help. The AAP advises a quick goodbye ritual, done the same way each day, and practice at being apart beforehand. It notes that daily separation worry rarely lasts beyond the preschool years.
By age 3, most children calm down within about 10 minutes after a parent leaves, for example at a childcare drop-off. Most also notice other children and join them to play.

anaya-school-bag.how_story_uses_it: Anaya's tummy is gurgling, and Basta turns each worry into a question with a clear answer: food is in the front pocket, crayons are here, and a name tag is in the secret pocket. Knowing what to expect helps. The biggest worry, "What if I have no friend?", gets a concrete plan: two biscuits, one to share. At school she offers one to a girl on the bench and makes her first friend.
anaya-school-bag.age_note: By 3, most children calm down within about 10 minutes after a parent leaves at drop-off. By 4, most ask to play with other children.
anaya-school-bag.try_tonight: Pack the bag together and name each pocket, like Basta. Then agree on a short goodbye ritual for tomorrow (for example, two hugs and a wave). Keep it the same every day and don't linger.
anaya-school-bag.doctor: Speak to your paediatrician if your child is not settling into separations or you are worried. The AAP notes that daily separation worry rarely continues past the preschool years.

anaya-brushu.skill: Toothbrushing habit formation (a nightly routine that protects baby teeth)
anaya-brushu.headline: Tooth decay in baby teeth is very common in India, and brushing twice a day with the right small amount of fluoride toothpaste, with a parent's help, is the best-proven way to prevent it.

findings.text: Tooth decay in young children is common in India. A review of 71 studies covering 69,330 Indian children found that 46.9% had early childhood caries (tooth decay in baby teeth).

Fluoride toothpaste works. A Cochrane review (a careful summary of all good trials) found high-certainty evidence that toothpaste with 1,000–1,250 ppm fluoride leads to less new decay than toothpaste without fluoride. Most of these trials looked at older children's permanent teeth.

The amount matters. The American Academy of Pediatrics says: under age 3, use only a smear the size of a grain of rice; from age 3, use a pea-sized amount. Brush twice a day, and parents should watch so the child doesn't use or swallow too much.

Many children get too much toothpaste. In a US survey of 5,157 children aged 3–15, more than 38% of the 3–6-year-olds used half a brush or a full brush of toothpaste — more than the pea-sized amount advised. Only about 60% of children aged 3–15 brushed twice a day.

Young children cannot yet brush well on their own. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry says young children 'do not have the ability to brush their teeth effectively', so parents should brush for them or help.

Habits grow by repeating the same action at the same time and place. In a study of 96 adults, a daily action became automatic after anywhere from 18 to 254 days, and missing one day did not really slow the habit down. This was studied in adults, not children, but the idea — same cue, every day — is the same.

anaya-brushu.how_story_uses_it: When Brushu says 'teeth never get a holiday', the story makes the key rule — brush every night — into a joke children remember. Brushing comes right after dinner, in the same bathroom, every time: that steady cue is how habits form. The talk prompt asks for just a small dot of toothpaste, which matches the pea-sized advice for children aged 3 and over.
anaya-brushu.age_note: At ages 3–5, children should use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, twice a day. They still need an adult to brush for them or help, because they cannot yet clean well on their own.
anaya-brushu.try_tonight: Brush in the same place right after dinner. Put a pea-sized dot of fluoride toothpaste on the brush and let your child brush first while you make Brushu's 'chik-chik-chik' sounds, then you go over every tooth yourself. Ask them to spit, and don't rinse with water afterwards.
anaya-brushu.doctor: The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry advises a first dental visit when the first tooth appears, or by the first birthday. If your child hasn't been yet, book one. The AAP also advises fluoride varnish on the teeth 2–4 times a year until age 5 — ask your doctor or dentist about it.

anaya-potty.skill: Toilet-training readiness (noticing body signals and acting on them), plus hand-washing
anaya-potty.headline: Children learn to use the potty best when they are ready and the adults around them stay calm and encouraging — and noticing the body's 'I need to go' signal is a key readiness sign.

findings.text: In the United States, toilet training usually starts between ages 2 and 3, and most children have full bowel and bladder control by age 4. Signs of readiness include staying dry for 2 hours and showing that a poo or wee is coming — like grunting, freezing or squatting.

Following the child's lead works for most children. In a classic 1962 study by Dr T. Berry Brazelton of 1,170 children trained with a 'child-oriented' approach (waiting until the child was interested and ready), children were dry in the daytime at an average age of 28.5 months. There is still no top-quality trial showing which training method is best.

Holding in poo is common. In one randomised trial of suburban children, 22% refused to do poo on the toilet at some point during training. The AAP explains that children aged 2 to 5 may hold back poo as a way of taking control, and that pressure during training can make this worse.

Praise works better than treats or scolding. The AAP advises praising what the child actually did ('I am so proud you used the toilet') rather than giving treats or punishments. One study summarised in a medical review found that children without ongoing wetting problems were more likely to have had parents who encouraged them to try again later, rather than punishing them. This shows a link, not proof of cause.

Hand-washing protects children's tummies. A Cochrane review of 29 randomised trials found that hand-washing programmes in child day-care centres and schools in high-income countries prevented about one-third of diarrhoea episodes (9 trials, 4,664 people), and community programmes in low- and middle-income countries probably prevented about one-quarter (9 trials, 15,950 people).

anaya-potty.how_story_uses_it: Anaya's tummy says 'गुड़-गुड़', and the story turns that body signal into a character children can listen to — the same 'I need to go' sign doctors look for. When Anaya tries to hold it in to finish her tower, the tummy 'wins', showing gently that it's better not to hold on. Pottu cheers for her try, which matches the advice to praise what the child did rather than use treats or scolding.
anaya-potty.age_note: Most children start between ages 2 and 3 and have full control by about age 4; in Brazelton's classic study, daytime dryness came at an average of 28.5 months. Accidents at ages 3–5 are still normal.
anaya-potty.try_tonight: When your child says their tummy is talking, stop what you're doing and go together. Afterwards, praise the try in plain words ('You listened to your tummy!'), with no treats and no scolding for accidents. Then wash hands with soap together.
anaya-potty.doctor: The AAP suggests talking about toilet training at the 18-month, 2-year, 2½-year and 3-year check-ups, and contacting your doctor about any worry before, during or after training. Talk to a doctor if poo is often hard, dry or painful, if you see blood, or if there are small poo streaks in underwear — and check with them before starting any constipation medicine.

seeti-kaka.skill: Overcoming food neophobia (trying new or disliked vegetables through repeated small tastes)
seeti-kaka.headline: Children often refuse new or green foods at first; tiny, repeated, pressure-free tastes are the best-proven way to help them like vegetables.

findings.text: Food neophobia means being unwilling to eat, or avoiding, new foods. It is a normal stage of childhood and one reason many children refuse vegetables.

Toddlers around age 2 are especially likely to avoid new foods, and this usually eases as they leave the toddler years. Some toddlers accepted a new vegetable after just 5 tastes, but children who refuse food very strongly needed as many as 27.

Tasting a little every day helps. In a randomised trial with 143 children aged 2–6, parents offered a tiny taste of a disliked vegetable every day for 14 days. Only this 'tasting' group showed clear gains in eating the vegetable, liking it and ranking it; a group that was only told about the vegetable did not show gains on all three.

Across 30 studies with 4,017 children aged 2–5, repeated tasting was the strongest method (a moderate effect), and about 8–10 tastes gave a moderate improvement. Tasting worked even better when combined with small rewards and adults eating the food too. Programmes run by parents worked better than those run by researchers. Teaching facts alone had the smallest effect.

Pressure backfires. In a small lab study, preschoolers ate more and made far fewer negative comments when they were not pushed to finish their food. The AAP warns that pushing or punishing children to eat can make them dislike foods.
The AAP says it can take 10 or more tastes before a young child accepts a new food, and suggests making food look fun and eating together as a family.

seeti-kaka.how_story_uses_it: Anaya's 'No green!' is typical food neophobia, not naughtiness. Seeti Kaka turns tasting into a game, with a whistle and a lid-clap for every green bite — small, cheerful tastes and praise, which are the parts research supports. Keep the 'race' light: the aim is one more small taste, not a clean plate, because pressure to finish can backfire.
seeti-kaka.age_note: Refusing new foods is strongest around age 2 and usually eases through ages 3–5. Many children need 8–10 or more small tastes of a vegetable before they accept it.
seeti-kaka.try_tonight: Put one tiny piece of the same green vegetable on your child's plate, and eat some yourself. Cheer ('सीईईटी!') for any lick or bite, and don't push for more. Offer that same vegetable again on many nights — about 8–10 tastes is when change usually shows.
seeti-kaka.doctor: The AAP advises that if you are worried about your child's diet, talk with your paediatrician, who can check that your child is getting all the nutrients they need.

dadi-quack.skill: Humour and incongruity (enjoying things that are 'wrong' on purpose), plus the helmet routine
dadi-quack.headline: Preschoolers love jokes built on 'wrong' things, like a horn that quacks, and laughing together may help them learn; the helmet check teaches a habit that greatly lowers the risk of serious head injury.

findings.text: Children make up their own jokes very early. In a study of 160 parents, children copied jokes in their first year and began making up new jokes from age 2; by age 3, most of their jokes were their own inventions.

Between ages 1 and 2, children start laughing at 'incongruity' (something that doesn't fit, like a hat on a dog), and from age 2 at silly words and wrong names. This is a normal stage of humour, and the review notes it can be held back when adults don't respond to a child's jokes.

Laughter may help learning. In a lab study of 53 babies aged 18 months, those who laughed at a funny demonstration copied a new action more often than babies who didn't laugh or who saw a plain demonstration. It was a small study with very young children, so treat it as a promising hint.

Helmets save lives. The WHO says correct helmet use can reduce the risk of death in a crash by more than 6 times and the risk of brain injury by up to 74%. A Cochrane review of 61 studies found that helmet wearers had about 69% lower odds of head injury and about 42% lower odds of death; those studies were mostly about adult riders. Road injuries are the leading cause of death for people aged 5–29.

In India, the Central Motor Vehicles (Second Amendment) Rules, 2022 say a child aged 9 months to 4 years riding on a two-wheeler must wear a crash helmet (or an approved bicycle helmet) and a safety harness, and the vehicle must not go faster than 40 km/h.

Knowing is not the same as doing. In a Delhi survey of 349 two-wheeler riders, 62.5% strongly agreed that children should wear helmets, but only 37.2% reported making sure children riding with them also wore helmets (a small survey on one hospital campus). In Bengaluru, researchers who watched 98,021 two-wheelers found that 88% of riders and pillion riders wore some helmet, but only 38% of riders wore it correctly.

dadi-quack.how_story_uses_it: The horn that says 'क्वैक' instead of 'पीं-पीं', and Dadi saying 'टो-क्वैक-टो', are the kind of 'wrong on purpose' jokes that children aged 2 and up find very funny. The helmet check ('Helmet पहना? Strap लगाया? टक!') happens before every ride, making it a routine rather than a lecture. Fastening the strap is part of wearing the helmet correctly, which WHO names as what protects.
dadi-quack.age_note: By age 2, children make up their own jokes, and by age 3 most of their jokes are their own. India's 2022 rule requires a helmet and harness for children aged 9 months to 4 years on two-wheelers.
dadi-quack.try_tonight: Take turns making silly horn sounds and laugh at each other's. Then practise Tinku's helmet check with a real helmet: helmet on, strap fastened ('टक!'), and check it doesn't slide around. Do this same check before every ride.

moti-meow.skill: Humour through mix-ups, and early vocabulary through animal sounds
moti-meow.headline: A dog that says 'meow' is a classic toddler joke: children need to know the right sound to find the wrong one funny, and animal-sound words are some of the easiest words for young children to learn.

findings.text: Mix-up jokes are among the first jokes children make. In a study of 160 parents of 2- and 3-year-olds, children's jokes included mislabelling things (calling a cat a dog) and 'pig says moo' jokes, and children made up new jokes from age 2.

Toddlers can tell a joke from a mistake. In a study of 78 toddlers aged 19–36 months, all ages copied the adult when a 'wrong' action was clearly a joke, but corrected it when it was clearly a mistake. From about 25 months, children also used the adult's laughter to tell that an unclear action was meant as a joke.

Sound-words help children learn words. In a study of about 2,000 English words, words that sound like what they mean (like 'moo' or 'woof') were learned earlier, used more often by young children, and used more by adults when talking to children.

In two experiments with 111 children, children learned names for new toys better when the name matched the sound the toy made. This benefit showed mainly in the 3-year-olds, less in the 18-month-olds.
From about age 2, children enjoy playing with language — silly words, changed song lyrics, and calling things by the wrong name on purpose. Warm adult responses help this kind of humour grow.

moti-meow.how_story_uses_it: Every time Moti tries to bark and says 'म्याऊँ', 'मूँ' or 'कुकड़ूँ-कूँ', your child gets to feel clever, because they know the right sound. Anaya laughing and naming each animal ('Moti cow बन गया!') shows it's a joke, not a mistake, and keeps pairing each animal with its real sound.
moti-meow.age_note: By about 2 years, children make up mix-up jokes like 'pig says moo', and from about 25 months they use an adult's laughter to tell a joke from a mistake. Sound-words like 'moo' and 'woof' are among the earliest words children learn.
moti-meow.try_tonight: Play the mix-up game: say 'The cow says… meow!' and laugh so your child knows it's a joke. Let them correct you ('No! Moo!'), then swap turns so they make the wrong sound and you correct them.

golu-chhupan-chhupai.skill: Early perspective-taking (understanding what someone else can see) and playful humour in hide-and-seek
golu-chhupan-chhupai.headline: Young children are famously bad at hiding because they are still learning how others see them; hide-and-seek lets them practise this while they laugh together.

findings.text: Many 3- and 4-year-olds think they are hidden if their eyes are covered, even though they know their head and body can still be seen. Researchers found they seem to believe that 'being seen' needs eyes to meet. In one experiment with 37 children, only 7 understood that they could see out through goggles while others could not see their eyes.
Laughing at peekaboo with a loved one is one of the earliest kinds of humour in the first two years, and children learn signals like big faces and funny voices that mean 'this is play'.

Children who can see a joke enjoy silly hiding. In a study of 78 toddlers aged 19–36 months, children from about 25 months used an adult's laughter to understand that an odd action was meant to be funny.
Object jokes, like wearing something on your head that doesn't belong there, were among the jokes that 2- and 3-year-olds invented themselves in a study of 160 parents.

The honest picture on pretend play: a major review found that current evidence 'does not support strong causal claims' that pretend play on its own drives development. Play is still a normal, joyful part of childhood, and the adults and conversations that come with it may matter just as much.

golu-chhupan-chhupai.how_story_uses_it: Golu hides behind a tiny tree with her horn, tail and tummy sticking out, and she's sure she's perfectly hidden. That is exactly the mistake 3- and 4-year-olds make, so your child gets to be the clever one who spots her. Her leaf 'cap' and the giggling pink blanket are object jokes that children this age love and invent themselves.
golu-chhupan-chhupai.age_note: At 3–4, many children still think covering their eyes hides them. Peekaboo-style laughter starts in the first two years, and children understand that silly actions are jokes from about 2 years.
golu-chhupan-chhupai.try_tonight: Play a quick game of hide-and-seek at home. When it's your turn to hide, hide badly on purpose, with a foot or elbow sticking out like Golu, and let your child find you. Laugh together and talk about what gave you away ('You saw my foot!').

pyasa-kauwa.skill: Causal reasoning and problem-solving (working out how things work), plus early counting
pyasa-kauwa.headline: Young children solve 'thirsty crow' puzzles by trying, noticing what works and trying again, and counting real objects out loud builds their sense of number.

findings.text: Scientists gave children a real version of the crow's problem: a small prize floating low in a tall tube, with water nearby. Only 8% of 4-year-olds thought of pouring water in to lift it up, compared with 42% of 6-year-olds and 58% of 8-year-olds (24 children in each age group). So if your preschooler cannot work it out yet, that is completely normal.

In a study of 80 children aged 4 to 10 given the crow's stone-dropping puzzle, 4- to 7-year-olds learned gradually over about five tries which tube to drop objects into. 4-year-olds did better than guessing only by the fifth try. From age 8, children solved it on the first try. For little children, learning comes from trying again.

Stepping in too fast can backfire. In two experiments with 150 children aged 4 to 5, children whose adult took over a hard puzzle gave up sooner on the next task than children who were shown how, or left to try on their own. It is one research group's work, but the experiments were planned and registered in advance.

Knowing that the last number you say tells you 'how many' takes time. In a classic study, only the older children (average age 3 and a half) answered 'how many?' with the last number they had counted most of the time. Younger children could say the numbers but did not yet link them to amount.

Counting things a child can see seems to matter most. In 44 families, parents who counted visible objects with their child at 14 to 30 months had children who understood numbers better at almost 4 years. Number talk without objects in view did not show this link, and counting bigger groups (4 to 10 things) mattered most. This shows a link, not proof of cause.

pyasa-kauwa.how_story_uses_it: The crow tries three ideas that fail (head in the pot, pushing the pot, asking the water nicely), stops, thinks, and then tries stones. That is the try-notice-try-again pattern young children use on real water puzzles. Each 'plink' gets one number, from one to ten, so your child hears one count for each object, in the 4-to-10 range that mattered most for number learning.
pyasa-kauwa.age_note: By age 5, most children can count to 10 (CDC). Understanding that the last number counted means 'how many' usually arrives around age 3 and a half to 4. Inventing the crow's trick without help is still hard at 4: only 8% of 4-year-olds managed it in one study.
pyasa-kauwa.try_tonight: Tomorrow, drop 10 pebbles, coins or buttons into a glass of water one at a time. Your child does the dropping and you count together, one number per drop, and watch the water rise. If they get stuck, give a hint rather than doing it for them.

kabootar-jaal.skill: Cooperation (working together towards a shared goal)
kabootar-jaal.headline: Children as young as 18 months can work with a partner towards a shared goal, and working together makes 3-year-olds share the reward more fairly.

findings.text: In a study of 32 toddlers aged 18 and 24 months, children happily joined an adult in two-person games and problem-solving tasks. When the adult suddenly stopped playing, every child tried at least once to bring the partner back, by looking, pointing or talking, as if to say 'we're doing this together'.

Working together changes how children share. In three experiments with 240 children aged 2 and 3, 3-year-olds who had worked together to earn prizes shared them much more fairly than when prizes simply appeared or when each child worked alone. In one experiment they evened out the prizes in 75% of team trials but only 25% of work-alone trials. 2-year-olds did not yet show this difference.

Children do not always find a story's lesson on their own. In a study of 96 children aged 5 and 6, 84% of children who were asked to explain why things happened in a story applied its lesson to a new real-life situation, compared with 63% of children who only retold what happened.

The Panchatantra is India's most famous collection of fables. Its Oxford translator describes it as teaching the principles of good government and wise conduct 'through the medium of animal tales', and one of its five books is about 'securing allies', which means making and keeping friends. Teaching through animal stories is a very old Indian method.

An Indian study of 60 rural children found higher scores on values such as cooperation, honesty and fairness after six weeks of storytelling sessions. The children were older (10 to 12) and the study was small, so it is a hopeful sign rather than proof for preschoolers.

kabootar-jaal.how_story_uses_it: When each pigeon flies alone (left, right, up) the net does not move, and even proud Guttu cannot lift it by himself. Only on 'one, two, three... fly!', with everyone at once, does the net rise. It falls back while one little pigeon is still eating, which shows that everyone's part counts. Then Chinki, a friend, helps them. The talk prompt asks your child to explain how the pigeons got free, and explaining is the step that helps children find a story's lesson.
kabootar-jaal.age_note: Toddlers of 18 to 24 months already join simple two-person games. Around age 3, working together makes children share the rewards more fairly. By age 5, most children can follow rules and take turns in games with other children (CDC).
kabootar-jaal.try_tonight: Tomorrow, do one small two-person job, like carrying a pillow or folding a bedsheet, on 'one, two, three!'. Afterwards, ask 'Why did it work when we did it together?' and let your child explain in their own words.

chanda-khargosh.skill: Generosity (prosocial giving, even when it costs you something)
chanda-khargosh.headline: Even toddlers feel happy when they give, and children copy the generosity they see in the adults around them.

findings.text: In one study, toddlers just under 2 years old looked happier when giving treats to a puppet than when getting treats themselves. They looked happiest when giving away a treat of their own rather than a spare one. It was a small study of 20 toddlers.

A larger 2026 study of 134 toddlers aged about 17 to 24 months found the same pattern. Toddlers showed more happiness after giving than after receiving, and giving to someone else made them happier than giving to themselves.

Giving when it costs you is hard when you are small. In a Swiss study of 229 children aged 3 to 8, only 8.7% of 3- and 4-year-olds chose to share equally when it meant giving up part of their own reward, compared with 45% of 7- and 8-year-olds.

Children in India learn giving by watching adults. In a study of 154 children aged 3 to 8 in rural Indian villages and 163 in a US city, the Indian children gave more after watching a parent give generously, and this effect grew with age. The US children did not change after a generous example. In both places, children gave less after watching a stingy one.

How a story ends matters. In a study of 268 children aged 3 to 7, a story that praised a child for doing the right thing (George Washington and the cherry tree) increased honest behaviour. Stories about being punished for lying (Pinocchio, The Boy Who Cried Wolf) did not.

One honest caution: stories about talking animals may teach less than stories about people. In one study, 4- to 6-year-olds gave more after a sharing story with human characters, but not after the same story told with animals. A 2023 Singapore study of 228 children aged 3 to 6 found a similar pattern for honesty in 3- and 4-year-olds. Linking the story to your child's own life afterwards is one way to bridge this gap.

chanda-khargosh.how_story_uses_it: This is a gentle retelling of the Sasa Jataka (No. 316), a Buddhist tale in which a hare with nothing else to offer gives himself to a hungry traveller and is honoured with his picture on the moon. In our version, Chhotu gives his last carrot, which is costly giving at a child's scale. The story ends with warmth and reward (the moon picture, three new carrots) rather than a warning, which is the kind of ending that helped children in the honesty-story research.
chanda-khargosh.age_note: Toddlers already enjoy giving. Giving up something of your own is still hard at 3 to 4 (8.7% chose to in one study), and it grows steadily through ages 5 to 8.
chanda-khargosh.try_tonight: Let your child see you give. Share part of your snack with someone at home and say simply why ('Dadi is hungry, so I'm sharing'). Then give your child a chance to give something of their own, and notice the happy feeling together.

sher-chuhiya.skill: Helping and reciprocity (kindness that is returned)
sher-chuhiya.headline: Children start helping others from about 18 months, and by about 3 and a half they begin to return kindness to people who were kind to them.

findings.text: In a classic study, 22 of 24 babies aged 18 months helped an adult who was struggling, for example by picking up something he had dropped. They did this without being asked or rewarded, and most helped within about 5 seconds.

Kindness coming back starts in the preschool years. In a study of 72 children, 3-and-a-half-year-olds shared more with a partner who had earlier shared with them. 2-and-a-half-year-olds did not yet do this. Being helped earlier did not change how much children helped back.

Rewards can crowd out kindness. When 20-month-olds were given a toy reward for helping, they later helped in only 53% of chances, compared with 81% for children who had been praised and 89% for children who got nothing (36 children).

Words matter, but results are mixed. In one study of 149 children aged 3 to 6, asking them to 'be a helper' led to more helping than asking them 'to help'. But a later study of 139 children aged 4 to 5 found that after a mistake, children asked to 'be helpers' felt worse and helped less. While your child is still learning, 'thank you for helping' may be the gentler choice.

sher-chuhiya.how_story_uses_it: Sheru lets Chuchu go for nothing in return; it is simply kind. Later Chuchu hears his roar, comes running and chews through the net, so kindness comes back, the way preschoolers begin to return kindness. Chuchu's tiny teeth show that small helpers can really help. The story ends in friendship, not a prize, which matches research showing that rewards can crowd out helping.
sher-chuhiya.age_note: Helping starts around 18 months. Returning kindness to someone who shared with you appears around 3 and a half. By age 5, most children can do simple chores at home, like matching socks or clearing the table (CDC).
sher-chuhiya.try_tonight: Tomorrow, give your child one real, small job, like carrying the spoons or finding your slippers. Thank them warmly with words and a hug instead of a sweet or a sticker.

khargosh-kachhua.skill: Persistence (keeping going on a hard or boring task)
khargosh-kachhua.headline: Children learn to keep going partly by watching others keep going, and pretending to be a determined character can help.

findings.text: Babies copy effort. In experiments with 262 babies about 15 months old, babies who watched an adult try several times before succeeding then pressed a hard toy's button about twice as often as babies who saw the adult succeed easily (a median of 18 presses against 9 in the repeat study). The effect was strongest when the adult looked at the baby and spoke to them directly.

In a study of 180 children aged 4 and 6, children did a boring task for 10 minutes with a fun video game nearby. Children who pretended to be a hard-working character, like Batman, worked the longest. The differences between groups were modest, but the pattern was the same at both ages.

Self-control matters, but less than once thought. A replication of the famous 'marshmallow test' found that each extra minute a 4-year-old waited predicted slightly better school results at 15. The link was only half the size first reported, and it shrank by two-thirds once family background and early abilities were taken into account.

Praising effort may help. In 53 families, parents who praised their 1- to 3-year-olds' effort had children who, at 7 to 8, more often believed that ability grows with hard work. Praise for being clever was not linked either way. It is one small study.

Keep expectations realistic. Two large reviews, the bigger one pooling 273 studies and 365,915 people, found that 'growth mindset' beliefs, and school programmes that teach them, have only weak effects on school results overall.

khargosh-kachhua.how_story_uses_it: Dheemi says her line again and again ('slowly, but don't stop'), so your child hears effort shown many times, as the babies saw in the research. Tez stops for carrots, a puddle and a nap, like the tempting video game in the Batman study, while Dheemi keeps working. At the end Tez says 'next time I won't stop', which puts the win down to effort, not speed.
khargosh-kachhua.age_note: Staying on a dull task grows a lot between 4 and 6: in one study, 6-year-olds stayed on task about 46% of the time and 4-year-olds about 28%. By age 5, most children can pay attention for 5 to 10 minutes during activities like story time (CDC).
khargosh-kachhua.try_tonight: Tomorrow, let your child see you try at something a little hard (a tight jar lid, a puzzle) and say out loud, 'This is hard... let me try another way', before you succeed. When your child keeps trying at something, praise the effort: 'You kept going, just like Dheemi!'

topiwala-bandar.skill: Emotion regulation (calming anger so you can think) and flexible problem-solving
topiwala-bandar.headline: Big angry feelings are normal at 3 to 5, and children learn to calm down and think by watching adults do it and by practising self-control in play.

findings.text: Tantrums are very common. Among 1,490 preschoolers aged 3 to 5, 83.7% had tantrums at least sometimes in the past month. Only 8.6% had them every day.

The American Academy of Pediatrics says tantrums happen most between ages 1 and 3 and tend to get better after 3. Its advice to parents is to do your best to stay calm, and to take a break or hand over to another adult when your own frustration rises.

Children are strong copiers. Children aged 2 to 6 in Brisbane, Australia and in Kalahari Bushman communities copied an adult's actions, even pointless ones, at about the same rate. Copying adults seems to be a way of learning shared by children everywhere.

Ages 3 to 5 bring fast growth in self-control skills (executive function, meaning the brain's skills for focusing, remembering rules and stopping yourself). Harvard's Center on the Developing Child suggests games like freeze dance, where children must stop and hold their bodies still.

Do such games work? In a randomised trial with 65 preschoolers, 16 sessions of circle-time games like 'Red Light, Purple Light' did not improve self-control for the group as a whole. They did help the children who started with the weakest self-control. The evidence is promising, not proven.

topiwala-bandar.how_story_uses_it: At first Chacha shakes his fist and stamps his foot, and the monkeys copy him, so anger gets him nowhere. Then he laughs, takes one long breath and thinks, and that is when the idea comes. The monkeys copy everything, the way young children copy the adults around them. The 'copy me' game in the talk prompt is also a playful way to practise watching and controlling your body.
topiwala-bandar.age_note: Tantrums are most frequent between 1 and 3 and usually ease after 3 (AAP), though 83.7% of 3- to 5-year-olds still have them sometimes. By age 5, most children can follow rules and take turns in games (CDC).
topiwala-bandar.try_tonight: Tomorrow, play 'copy me', then add a freeze rule: when you say 'statue!', everyone stops still. And next time you feel cross, let your child see you calm yourself the way Chacha did: stop, take one slow breath, and then say what you will do.
topiwala-bandar.doctor: Talk to your child's doctor if tantrums often involve hurting themselves or others, breaking things or holding their breath; if they are getting longer or more severe or happen several times a day; if they still happen regularly after age 5; or if you are feeling very stressed handling them.

lal-murgi.skill: Helping at home (prosocial helping) and sharing fairly after working together
lal-murgi.headline: Toddlers want to help from about 18 months, and children as young as 3 share more fairly after they have done a job together, so small real jobs at home are the best teacher.

findings.text: Helping starts early. In a classic experiment, 22 of 24 babies aged 18 months helped an adult stranger reach a goal at least once, without being asked or rewarded.

In an online survey of over 500 families, parents said their 4-year-olds joined in about 5 out of 9 common chores, such as putting away toys, throwing away trash and helping with dishes. Most parents also said this help is sometimes more mess than help. That is normal, not a sign the child is doing it wrong.

Treats can backfire. In 36 toddlers aged about 20 months, those who got a small prize for helping later helped in 53% of chances, compared with 89% for toddlers who got nothing and 81% for toddlers who got a warm 'thank you'.

In 207 children aged 5 to 13, those who did more chores such as making meals had better working memory (holding things in mind) and self-control, by parent report. This study looked at older children and shows a link, not proof that chores cause the change.

Working together changes how children share. Children of about 3 years shared rewards much more equally with a partner after they had worked for them together than when the same rewards just fell into their lap.

lal-murgi.how_story_uses_it: Kukdu does every step herself (sowing, cutting, grinding, cooking) while Mani says 'Not me!', so the child sees how much work a roti takes. When Mani finally brings water and plates, Kukdu breaks the roti in two and they eat together, which matches the finding that children share more equally after a shared effort. Mani's 'next time, me!' ending shows helping as something to join in, not a punishment.
lal-murgi.age_note: Most children like to be a 'helper' by age 4, and by age 5 most do simple chores at home, like matching socks or clearing the table after eating (CDC).
lal-murgi.try_tonight: Give your child one real kitchen job tonight, like washing a tomato or carrying spoons to the table, and say a warm 'thank you, you helped' instead of giving a sweet as a reward. Then eat together and name what they did.

bandar-magar-jamun.skill: Cognitive flexibility (switching to a new plan when the old one fails), part of executive function
bandar-magar-jamun.headline: Changing plans under pressure is a brain skill that grows fast between ages 3 and 5, and young children can borrow a clever solution from a story, especially when a grown-up links it to real life.

findings.text: Executive function (the brain's 'air traffic control' for planning, remembering and self-control) grows at a fast pace between ages 3 and 5. The Harvard Center on the Developing Child recommends storytelling and games that switch rules to practise it.
Switching rules is hard for small children. In a classic card-sorting game, most 3-year-olds keep using the old rule after being told to change it, while by age 5 most children switch.

Children can use a solution they saw in a story. In 72 toddlers, 2.5-year-olds who watched a short video of a character using a tool to reach a goal chose the right tool first on about half of new problems. It worked only when the video showed both the character's goal and the action.

In 108 children aged 3 to 5, 72% used a lesson from a realistic story in real life, but only 24% did when the same lesson came in a fantasy story. Children get better at telling the two apart between ages 3 and 5.

An honest limit: in a study of 4- to 6-year-olds, a sharing story with human characters made children share more, while the same story told with talking animals did not. So it helps when a parent links an animal story back to the child's own life.

Pretending to be a clever character can help children keep going. In 180 children aged 4 and 6, those asked to pretend to be a hero such as Batman stuck with a boring task longest, compared with children who thought about themselves.

bandar-magar-jamun.how_story_uses_it: In the middle of the river Chintu realises he is in trouble, but he does not cry: he stops, thinks ('hmm... hmm... ting! Idea!') and switches plan by saying his golden jamun is back on the tree. The story shows the goal (get home safely) and the action (a clever excuse, then a big jump) together, which is the kind of example young children can learn from. The closing line, 'think with a cool head', gives the child words to use later.
bandar-magar-jamun.age_note: Most 3-year-olds still stick to an old rule after being told to switch; by about age 5 most can switch (Zelazo 2006). The AAP notes that 3- to 4-year-olds often see a problem from only one point of view.
bandar-magar-jamun.try_tonight: Ask 'How did Chintu get back to his tree?', then link it to real life: 'What could you do if you got stuck somewhere?' Tomorrow, play a quick sorting game (sort toys by colour, then switch to sorting by size) to practise changing plans.

birbal-khichdi.skill: Fairness based on effort (merit) and keeping promises
birbal-khichdi.headline: Children start to feel that 'the one who worked should get the reward' from about age 3, and they watch closely whether grown-ups keep their word.

findings.text: By about age 3, when children share rewards between two workers, they already prefer that the harder worker gets more, as a 2023 study summarises from earlier experiments.

In 72 children aged 3 and 5, children kept more stickers when they had done more of the work. But few gave away more than half when their partner had worked harder, so being fair to others takes longer than being fair to yourself.
In sharing games, most 3- to 4-year-olds chose selfishly, while most 7- to 8-year-olds chose splits that were equal for both children.
What counts as fair is partly learned from culture. Children in a Western city shared by how much each person worked, while children in two African communities did not use work as the main rule.
Promises matter to small children. In 145 German children aged 3 and 5, both ages strongly refused to break their own promises, whatever the reason.

Children notice whether grown-ups keep their word. In 28 children aged 3.5 to 5.8, those who had just seen an adult keep a promise waited an average of 12 minutes for a second treat, compared with about 3 minutes after an adult broke one. A larger repeat study (60 children) found the same direction but a much smaller difference: 9.6 versus 7.0 minutes.

birbal-khichdi.how_story_uses_it: Champa keeps her side of the deal and stands in the cold pond all night, but Akbar refuses to pay because she looked at a far-away diya. Birbal's pot hung high above a tiny fire makes the unfairness easy for a small child to see and laugh at. When Akbar pays the hundred coins and adds a warm shawl, the story ends on 'give people what they have truly earned'.
birbal-khichdi.age_note: Children aged 3 to 5 already take effort into account, but mostly when it benefits them; choosing equal or fair splits that cost them something becomes common only around ages 7 to 8 (Fehr 2008). Refusing to get more than a friend appears later still, and not in every culture (Blake 2015).
birbal-khichdi.try_tonight: Keep one small promise to your child tonight exactly as you said it (for example, 'two more pages, then lights off'), and name it: 'I said two pages, and I kept my promise.' Tomorrow, after a job you do together, let your child share out the snack and ask, 'Who did what? What is fair?'

chidiya-dal-dana.skill: Persistence (keep trying after 'no') and asking for help politely
chidiya-dal-dana.headline: Children learn to keep trying partly by watching others try hard, and a long repeating chain like Chuski's helps them remember and retell the story.

findings.text: Babies copy effort. In 182 babies aged 15 months, those who watched an adult try hard and then succeed pressed the button on a new toy about twice as many times as babies who saw the adult succeed easily.
Words matter too. In two small studies of 18-month-olds, babies whose parents praised their effort ('you're trying so hard') kept trying longer on a tricky task, even when the parent was not helping.

In 151 children aged 3 to 5, children could often predict when they would need help with a new puzzle box, but they did not always ask for it. Knowing how and whom to ask is a skill children are still building.
Retelling helps. Kindergarten children who retold a story after hearing it understood it a little better, and the benefit grew with practice and adult guidance.

chidiya-dal-dana.how_story_uses_it: Chuski asks the carpenter, the King, the Queen, the mouse and finally Billu the cat, and each time she hears 'no' she says 'I won't give up' and politely tries someone else. The repeating chain ('please nudge the mouse... the mouse tickles the Queen...') models polite asking and is easy to retell. Chuski thanks every helper at the end, showing that asking for help and saying thank you go together.
chidiya-dal-dana.age_note: By age 4 most children can tell what comes next in a well-known story, and by age 5 most can retell a story they heard with at least two events (CDC).
chidiya-dal-dana.try_tonight: Tomorrow, take turns retelling Chuski's chain, from the cat back to the carpenter. When your child gets stuck on something real, praise the trying, not the result: 'You kept asking so nicely, and you didn't give up.'

badi-mooli.skill: Cooperation and teamwork (working towards a shared goal)
badi-mooli.headline: Even toddlers treat a shared task as 'ours', and children share more fairly after they pull together, which is exactly what this cumulative tale shows.

findings.text: In 32 children aged 18 and 24 months, every child tried to get an adult partner back into a joint game when he stopped playing. The 3 young chimpanzees tested never did.
3-year-olds who worked together actively with a peer to get rewards then shared them mostly equally, even when one child could have kept more.

Repeating the same story helps small children remember. In a small study of 16 three-year-olds, children who heard the same stories again and again remembered new words a week later, while those who heard different stories did not.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says that rough-and-tumble play lets children take risks in a relatively safe way and builds communication, negotiation and emotional balance.

badi-mooli.how_story_uses_it: Dadaji cannot pull the radish out alone, so Dadi, Anaya, the dog, the cat and at last tiny Chinki the mouse join the chain, and the repeated 'pull... pull... pull!' lets the child join in and remember the order. When everyone tumbles into a heap and the radish pops out, the smallest helper is thanked and gets the first paratha, which matches the finding that children share with everyone who helped.
badi-mooli.age_note: By age 3 most children notice other children and join them to play; by age 5 most follow rules or take turns in games with other children (CDC).
badi-mooli.try_tonight: Tomorrow, ask 'Who helped last, and who was the smallest?' Then play a gentle tug-of-war with a dupatta, pulling together against a grown-up and falling onto a pillow, so your child feels how many small pulls add up.

chamku-diwali.skill: Family rituals and belonging, plus early counting (knowing that 'five' means five things)
chamku-diwali.headline: Shared festival rituals help children feel part of a group, and counting real things like diyas with a parent is one of the best-supported ways to build number sense before school.

findings.text: Rituals bring children together. In 71 children aged 4 to 11, those who made necklaces in a set, repeated 'ritual' way felt closer to their group than children who did the same craft without the ritual.

Many children can say 'one, two, three...' long before they understand it. Around age 2 they can often recite numbers but cannot give you 'three' of something; children usually understand what counting is for around their fourth birthday.

Parent number talk varies a lot and it matters. In 44 families observed for about 7.5 hours at home, parents said between 4 and 257 number words. More number talk predicted better understanding of numbers at about 46 months, even after allowing for family background.

Playing a simple number board game for about 1 hour in total improved low-income preschoolers' (average age 5.4) counting, reading of numbers, and judging which number is bigger, and the gains lasted 9 weeks. The same game with colours instead of numbers did not help.

In India, the ASER 2019 Early Years survey tested 36,930 children aged 4 to 8 in 24 states. Grade 1 children who could do sorting, ordering and pattern tasks did better at reading and at spoken number problems.
