chamku-diwali.how_story_uses_it: Chamku mistakes diyas for shy fireflies, and Anaya explains why we light them (to welcome Ram ji home) and why we share sweets, so the ritual comes with a reason. Anaya counts the diyas one to five, Chamku jumbles it to 'ten', and then they count properly and add Chamku to make six, which is the kind of object counting that builds number sense. When Chamku flies near a diya and finds it warm, he quickly moves back, a gentle safety lesson.
chamku-diwali.age_note: The AAP says 3- to 4-year-olds understand the idea of counting and may know a few numbers. By age 5 most children count to 10 and name some numbers between 1 and 5 when you point (CDC). By age 3 most children avoid touching hot things like a stove when warned (CDC).
chamku-diwali.try_tonight: On Diwali night, count the diyas together, touching or pointing to each one as you say the number, and end by asking 'So how many diyas?' Then share one sweet and say why we share it.
chamku-diwali.doctor: For a small burn, run cool water over it (the AAP suggests about five minutes), do not use ice, butter or home remedies, and cover it with a clean non-stick bandage. Get medical help straight away for any burn bigger than your child's hand, a burn on the hand, foot, face, genitals or a joint, or skin that looks charred, leathery or has no feeling. If you are worried about any burn, see a doctor.

mochi-chhote-madadgar.skill: Gratitude and reciprocity (giving back to someone who helped you)
mochi-chhote-madadgar.headline: From about age 3½, children give more to people who were kind to them first, and feeling grateful makes young children kinder, both to the giver and to others.

findings.text: In 72 children, 3.5-year-olds shared more toys with a partner who had shared with them before, while 2.5-year-olds shared the same with everyone. 'Giving back' seems to switch on around age 3½.
In 263 children followed from age 3 to 5, those who understood feelings better at 3, and thoughts better at 4, understood gratitude better at 5.
In three experiments with 388 children aged 3 to 6, children who had just received a gift helped and shared more with the giver, and were also more likely to help a stranger.
In 80 children with an average age of 5, those who were more grateful for specific things in their lives were happier. This shows a link, not cause and effect.
In a small focus-group study, 20 parents of 6- to 9-year-olds described gratitude as more than saying thank you: it has thinking, feeling and doing parts, and it grows slowly over childhood.

In 221 children aged about 12, writing down things they were grateful for over 2 weeks raised gratitude and lowered bad feelings, but did not make them more helpful. This was in older children, so we do not yet know how well it works at 3 to 5.

mochi-chhote-madadgar.how_story_uses_it: The tiny elves quietly make shoes every night, and Mochi Dada and Amma first notice the help, then wonder who it is, then feel sorry that the elves have no shoes of their own. They then do something about it: they sew tiny jackets and shoes and leave a thank-you card, so gratitude moves from noticing and feeling to doing, as parents in research describe it. The elves' happy dance shows the child that giving back feels good for both sides.
mochi-chhote-madadgar.age_note: Children start giving back to people who were kind to them at around 3½ (Warneken 2013), and understanding what gratitude means grows between ages 3 and 5, alongside understanding feelings (Nelson 2013).
mochi-chhote-madadgar.try_tonight: Tomorrow, think of one person who helps your family (a didi, a watchman, a grandparent) and make them a small thank-you card together. Walk through it: 'What did they do for us? How did that help? How does that make us feel? What can we do to say thanks?'

anaya-christmas-star.skill: Making things together (joint attention and shared goals) and the joy of giving
anaya-christmas-star.headline: Young children try harder and enjoy a task more when they feel they are doing it together, and even toddlers show more joy when they give than when they get.

findings.text: In 70 children aged 4 to 5, just being told they were working 'together' with someone made them stick longer with a hard puzzle and like it more, even though each child was actually working alone.
Toddlers aged about 23 months looked happier when giving a treat to a puppet than when getting one, and happiest when they gave away one of their own treats (a small study of 20 toddlers).

The Harvard Center on the Developing Child explains that 'serve and return' (back-and-forth moments between a child and a caring adult) helps build brain connections, and that naming what a child is seeing, doing or feeling helps make language connections.

A review of 50 years of research (32 publications) found family routines and rituals linked with more confident parenting and better child adjustment. The authors warn that many studies were small or used convenience samples.

anaya-christmas-star.how_story_uses_it: When Moti's search turns up a sock, a ball and then a star-shaped cookie that he gobbles, Anaya does not give up; she decides 'we will make a new star ourselves' with paper, glue and glitter. Anaya cannot reach the top alone and Moti's back wobbles, so Chamku flies the star up and lights it, and Anaya says 'we made it together'. The old star is then shared on the window so Chamku can find his way, turning the making into a gift.
anaya-christmas-star.age_note: The AAP says 3- to 4-year-olds can use child-safe scissors, copy squares and draw circles, and by age 4 most children hold a crayon between fingers and thumb (CDC), so cutting a simple star with help is well within reach.
anaya-christmas-star.try_tonight: Tomorrow, cut a simple paper star together with child-safe scissors. Let your child do what they can, talk about what they are doing ('you're cutting the pointy corner!'), and then choose together where to put it or whom to give it to.
